item.title: Configuring vex (config.lua)
item.description: .vex/config.lua returns a Lua table and is read on every command, after the global folder’s config.lua (see Configuring vex (config.lua) > The global folder). Settings you leave out take the defaults. vex init writes this one into .vex/config.lua:

item.title: Configuring views
item.description:
Each .lua file in .vex/views can register views. A view is a display function that takes the focus and the command’s flags and returns the text to print:

 view:view 'count' {
 display = function(focus, flags)
 return #focus:get() .. ' tasks'
 end
}
 
vex view all count

focus:get() returns the focus’s tasks. Read any field from them, transients included. Flags arrive as a table: vex view all count --field status gives flags.field == 'status'.

item.title: Configuring task types
item.description:
Each .lua file in .vex/tasks can register task types and transients.

Task types link

A type extends an existing one and adds a schema. Its schema is merged over its ancestors’: a field it defines replaces the ancestor’s definition of that field, and it inherits every other field. Its tasks must pass the merged schema:

 task:task 'bug':extends 'atom' {
 schema = schema.atleast {
 severity = schema.any {'low', 'high'},
 reported = schema.maybe {schema.formatted {schema.datetime}},
 }
}
 
vex add Crash on start --vextype bug --severity high

A schema validates, normalises, derives and converts a task’s fields each time it is resolved. Build yours from these blocks, among others:

item.title: Configuring recipes
item.description:
Each .lua file in .vex/recipes can register recipes. A recipe is an add function that receives the task manager and the properties from the command line, and adds tasks:

 recipe:recipe 'chore' {
 add = function(task, taskproperties)
 taskproperties.vextype = 'atom'
 return {task:add(taskproperties)}
 end
}
 
vex recipe chore Take out the bins

taskproperties holds the description and every flag. add returns the list of vexids it added. A recipe can add as many tasks as it likes and link them through their fields; vex resolves and writes each returned task in the order of the list, then focuses on all of them:

item.title: Configuring focuses
item.description:
Each .lua file in .vex/focuses can register named focuses. A named focus is a function that returns a list of tasks, usually built from other focuses:

 focus.register_focus('mine', function()
 return focus.focus('all'):filter('owner', 'alice'):filter('status', 'done'):get()
end)
 
vex focus mine --select due
vex view mine kanban

item.title: Configuring event hooks
item.description:
Each .lua file in .vex/events can register hooks. Every event comes in a pair: pre-<event> fires before the action and post-<event> after it. For example, pre-verb-set fires before the vex set command runs, and post-task-resolve fires after a task resolves. A hook receives the event’s args (see the table below):

 event:on 'post-task-resolve' (function(vexid, t)
 if t.due and t.due < os.time() and t.phase ~= 'final' then
 print(vexid .. ' is overdue')
 end
end)

A hook that raises an error stops the command. vex prints which hook failed, on which event, and why, for example Event hook 'needs-owner' failed on 'pre-verb-set': .... A pre- hook can therefore enforce project rules before anything changes, for example requiring every task to have an owner:
